problems.A: A maintainer has 300 abandoned prototype notes and ten minutes on Monday. Design a way to spot an unexpected combination worth building in one afternoon. The system may process each note once when added, and the maintainer can open only four notes on Monday.
problems.B: Two volunteers build separate halves of an interactive science exhibit and meet only on installation day. Their halves should produce a surprising interaction together. They can exchange one postcard each in advance, and either half might arrive late. Design how they collaborate.
problems.C: A neighborhood instrument library owns twenty little-used instruments and has one hour with a group of beginners. Design a borrowing session where people discover an instrument they would never have chosen and still feel confident taking it home. There is one facilitator and no app.
problems.D: An AI assistant helps a designer explore an idea across six short sessions. The designer wants genuinely different directions on each return, can read only two old passages per visit, and sometimes wants to recover a discarded direction exactly. Design the interaction.

reader: Using only the supplied material, propose two meaningfully different designs. Develop the more promising one with a concrete example and a cheap test that could distinguish it from a simpler alternative. Maximize useful originality. Maximum 110 whitespace-delimited words, including headings, per problem. Treat each problem independently. Do not mention prompts, notes, or the study.
selection: Three notes per problem from the project vault. Use each note's opening prose up to 650 UTF-8 bytes, at a whitespace boundary, with its title; same extraction for search and selected. Count the total source bytes. For search, rank titles and opening prose using FTS5 BM25 with the project's flat vault search stopwords and Porter tokenizer. Relabel the same selected sources to build the fourth condition. Each independent reader session sees all four problems under one condition, once, with rotated order. Repeats use fresh sessions. Use the same generation instructions and word ceiling for all conditions.
scoring: Three independent Codex reviewers see only anonymous answers grouped by problem. Randomize order separately per reviewer. Originality (primary), feasibility, and discriminating test (secondary) are each scored 1..5. For originality: 1 generic familiar pattern; 3 a meaningful adaptation; 5 a surprising, intelligible mechanism distinctive even among these designs. For feasibility: 1 breaks constraints; 3 plausible with gaps; 5 a workable concrete plan within stated resources. For test: 1 uninformative or absent; 3 names a comparison with a measurable result; 5 isolates the mechanism with a fair simple baseline and an outcome that could disfavor it. Average repeated generations and judges per problem, then weight problems equally. Report scores by condition, per-problem differences, review agreement and selection time. Exploratory, no claims about population significance. Readers and reviewers are AI. No human note-selection timing.
budget: Design generation ceiling 110 words per problem. For an overrun retain only the first 110 words for anonymous review and log the overrun. A label costs additional input text. Question-only is intentionally shorter. Measure wall time for a Codex curator to choose and label the notes from the catalog, and separately local search selection time. Packet creation, design generation, and scoring are outside the curator timer.
